note: Jude calls himself a servant first, then brother—not leading with his family tie to Jesus, but his choice to serve Him. There's wisdom in that order. He writes to the called and kept, reminding them their security rests on God's work, not their own grip.
Mercy, peace, love—multiplied. Not stingy sprinklings, but overflow. Jude opens his letter the way you'd wish someone on a hard road: with abundance, not scraps.

He wanted to write on salvation—the common inheritance—but felt the Spirit press him to fight for the faith. Sometimes our gentler plans must yield when a shore needs defending. The "faith once for all delivered" echoes Ephesians; there's a deposit we keep, not remake.

"Crept in secretly"—the danger isn't bold enemies but quiet ones, those who slip past the watchmen remaking grace into permission for anything. Jude names what they deny: Christ as Master and Lord. That's what's at stake.
Saved from Egypt, yet many perished in the wilderness for unbelief. A hard mercy: deliverance is not the same as faith. You can be held by God's hand and still fall away by refusing to trust Him.

Angels who abandoned their post—kept now in darkness for judgment. There's a warning here about authority: even the mighty can fall when they reject their charge. Our obedience, however humble, is never small.

Sodom and Gomorrah "going after strange flesh"—Jude names sexual sin as a tangible rebellion, not an abstraction. The cities stand as warning: when we exchange the Lord's design for appetite's whisper, judgment follows.
They defile the flesh in their dreams, despise authority, slander the celestial. It starts in thought—the dream becomes deed. How we speak about those in power, those unseen, shapes what we become.

Michael contending with the devil over Moses' body—a real moment from Jewish tradition—yet Michael does not curse the devil, only appeals to the Lord. Even in dispute with the adversary, restraint and deference to God's judgment remain.
They slander what they don't know, destroyed by what they do know—their own natural lusts, like beasts. There's a tragic irony: ignorance paired with arrogance makes a fool's foundation.

The way of Cain (envious violence), the error of Balaam (greed masked as prophecy), Korah's rebellion (presuming the office). Three old stories, one pattern: refusing God's order and paying the price.

Hidden reefs at the feast, shepherds who feed themselves, clouds and autumn trees all bereft. Jude piles image upon image—all false promise, all destructive. Leaders who exploit the flock are a special tragedy.
Wild waves foaming their shame, wandering stars in reserved darkness. They leave a mark—shame visible and recorded. Judgment is not hidden; it is written in the heavens.
Enoch, seventh from Adam, prophesied the Lord's coming with ten thousands of holy ones—a citation from the Book of Enoch, showing Jude's reach into ancient prophecy to warn his own generation.
Enoch's word continues: judgment on all, conviction of the ungodly. Their works, their ways, their words—all recorded. There is no hiding from Him who sees the whole.
Murmurers and complainers, walking after lust, proud mouths, showing favor for gain. A portrait of those who live by appetite and advantage—hollow inside.
But you, beloved—the tone shifts. Jude turns to the faithful, calling them to remember what the apostles taught. There's an anchor in the word spoken long ago, before the false ones arrived.
"In the last time there will be mockers"—a saying handed down from the apostles themselves. They saw the pattern coming; now Jude says, you are seeing it happen. Trust what was spoken.
Divisive, sensual, without the Spirit—the mockers become hollow, split from one another and from God's breath. When we lose the Spirit, we become architects of our own smallness.
Build yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit. Jude's prescription: steadiness, prayer, the Spirit's guidance. Growth is not against the false but toward the true.

Keep yourselves in God's love, looking for mercy unto eternal life. The stance is not anxious striving but rest—staying in the love He has already given, waiting for His compassion to complete the work.
Have compassion, making a distinction—mercy is not blind, but it is not cruel either. Some are caught in error and can be reached; the call is to see them and intercede.
Snatch some from the fire with fear, hating even the garment stained by sin. The work of rescue is urgent and costly; we must hate the corruption without losing sight of the one corrupted.
Able to keep them from stumbling and to present them faultless—the promise belongs to Him. Our defense is never our own steadiness but His keeping power and His willingness to cover our shame.

Readers today hear an echo in these closing words: God alone wise, glory and majesty, dominion and power now and forever. In a world of loud claims and false prophets, this doxology reminds us where all true authority rests—with the One who needs no defending but deserves our worship.
